intro: の turns what comes before it into a description of a noun. Between two nouns, A の B means "B, of the A kind": B is the thing, A narrows it down. After a verb or adjective, の wraps the action up so it can be used as a noun; with no noun after it, の stands in for one you have already mentioned; inside a clause before a noun it can mark the subject; and at the end of a sentence, のです wraps the whole statement up as an explanation. The thing always comes last, and everything before の describes it.

skills.rule: A の B: B is the thing, A tells you whose, which, where or what kind.
skills.explain:
Put の between two nouns and the second becomes the head: 私の本 is a book (mine), while 本の私 would be a me that belongs to the book. English "X's Y" and "the Y of X" both come out as X の Y, so the order is the reverse of "of": the owner, place, maker or material goes first. The link is broad: possession (母の傘), origin (日本の車), location (駅の前), topic (日本語の先生) and apposition (友達の田中さん, "my friend Tanaka"). You can chain it: 私の兄の車.

の joins nouns only. い-adjectives attach directly (大きい家) and な-adjectives take な (静かな部屋). A verb or a whole clause also attaches directly with no の: 昨日買った本.

When a phrase ending in another particle describes a noun, add の after that particle: 友達からの手紙, 東京での生活. Without の the particle phrase would attach to the verb instead.
patterns: [noun] から / で / へ / と の [noun]
[noun A] の [noun B] の [noun C]

examples.jp: 私[わたし]{の}本[ほん]です。
examples.en: It's my book.

examples.jp: これは母[はは]{の}傘[かさ]です。
examples.en: This is my mother's umbrella.

examples.jp: 日本[にほん]{の}車[くるま]は高[たか]いですか。
examples.en: Are Japanese cars expensive?

examples.jp: 駅[えき]{の}前[まえ]で待[ま]っています。
examples.en: I'm waiting in front of the station.

examples.jp: 友達[ともだち]{の}田中[たなか]さんを紹介[しょうかい]します。
examples.en: Let me introduce my friend, Mr Tanaka.

examples.jp: 友達[ともだち]から{の}手紙[てがみ]を読[よ]みました。
examples.en: I read the letter from my friend.

contrast.note: わたしは ほん makes わたし a topic and still needs a predicate (わたしは ほんを よみます). わたしの ほん is a single noun phrase, "my book", that can sit anywhere a noun can.
な links a な-adjective to a noun (しずかな へや); の links a noun to a noun (がくせいの へや). Words like びょうき are nouns, so it is びょうきの ひと.

mistakes.bad: 大[おお]きい{の}家[いえ]に住[す]んでいます。
mistakes.good: 大[おお]きい家[いえ]に住[す]んでいます。
mistakes.note: い-adjectives sit directly before the noun; no の.

mistakes.bad: 昨日[きのう]買[か]った{の}本[ほん]を読[よ]みました。
mistakes.good: 昨日[きのう]買[か]った本[ほん]を読[よ]みました。
mistakes.note: A verb clause modifies a noun directly; の only joins nouns.

mistakes.bad: これは本[ほん]{の}友達[ともだち]です。
mistakes.good: これは友達[ともだち]{の}本[ほん]です。
mistakes.note: 本の友達 means "a book friend". For "my friend's book" the owner goes first and the book, the thing you mean, goes last.

skills.tip: Two nouns in a row? The one you are talking about goes last, and の goes between. An adjective or a verb in front? No の.

skills.rule: Plain verb or adjective + の turns an action or state into a noun: "the doing of it".
skills.explain:
A verb cannot take が or を on its own, so to say "I like swimming" Japanese wraps the verb in の first: 泳ぐのが好きです. The verb stays in plain form and keeps its own objects and tense (本を読むの, 鍵をかけたの). After a noun or な-adjective, use なの: 静かなのが好き.

The particle after の comes from the predicate: 好き, 嫌い, 上手, 下手, 得意 take のが; 忘れる, 手伝う, 待つ, 見る, 聞く take のを; のは introduces a judgement (話すのは難しい).

こと does the same job, and often either is fine. The edge: の is for a concrete event you see, hear or take part in, and it is required with perception verbs (歌うのを聞いた, 走っているのが見える) and with 手伝う and 待つ. こと is for an idea or a fact stated as such, and it is required before です in definitions (趣味は本を読むことです) and in the fixed patterns ことができる, ことがある, ことにする.
patterns: [plain verb] の が 好き / 上手 / 嫌い
[plain verb] の を 見る / 聞く / 忘れる / 手伝う
[plain verb] の は [adjective] です

examples.jp: 泳[およ]ぐ{の}が好[す]きです。
examples.en: I like swimming.

examples.jp: 母[はは]は料理[りょうり]を作[つく]る{の}が上手[じょうず]です。
examples.en: My mother is good at cooking.

examples.jp: 日本語[にほんご]で話[はな]す{の}は難[むずか]しいです。
examples.en: Speaking in Japanese is hard.

examples.jp: 鍵[かぎ]をかける{の}を忘[わす]れました。
examples.en: I forgot to lock the door.

examples.jp: 子供[こども]たちが歌[うた]う{の}を聞[き]きました。
examples.en: I heard the children singing.

examples.jp: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]しを手伝[てつだ]う{の}は大変[たいへん]でした。
examples.en: Helping with the move was hard work.

contrast.note: こと names an idea or fact; の names an event as it happens. しゅみは よむことです (not のです), よむことが できます (not のが). But うたうのを ききました (not ことを): you hear an event, not an idea.
が cannot follow a bare verb: およぐが すきです is ungrammatical. The verb must be made a noun first, and then が marks it: およぐのが すきです.

mistakes.bad: 泳[およ]ぐ{が}好[す]きです。
mistakes.good: 泳[およ]ぐ{の}が好[す]きです。
mistakes.note: A verb needs の before a particle can attach to it.

mistakes.bad: 子供[こども]たちが歌[うた]う{こと}を聞[き]きました。
mistakes.good: 子供[こども]たちが歌[うた]う{の}を聞[き]きました。
mistakes.note: With verbs of seeing and hearing, the event takes の, never こと.

mistakes.bad: 趣味[しゅみ]は写真[しゃしん]を撮[と]る{の}です。
mistakes.good: 趣味[しゅみ]は写真[しゃしん]を撮[と]る{こと}です。
mistakes.note: Defining something with ...です takes こと; のです here would be read as an explanation.

skills.tip: Seeing, hearing, helping or waiting while it happens? の. A definition before です, or できる / ある / にする after it? こと.

skills.rule: With no noun after it, の means "one": the thing you both already have in mind.
skills.explain:
When the noun is obvious from context, Japanese drops it and keeps の in its place: 赤いの "the red one", 安いの "a cheaper one", 昨日買ったの "the one I bought yesterday". It attaches like a noun: い-adjectives and verbs directly, な-adjectives with な (静かなの).

After a noun, の already links to the missing noun, so "mine" is 私の, never 私のの: この傘は私のです.

The edge with もの: もの means "a thing" in general, so 赤いものをください asks for something red, any red thing. の points at a particular item in front of you or already mentioned. For people, use 人 or 方 instead: calling a person の sounds offhand.

examples.jp: 赤[あか]い{の}をください。
examples.en: The red one, please.

examples.jp: この傘[かさ]は私[わたし]{の}です。
examples.en: This umbrella is mine.

examples.jp: もっと安[やす]い{の}はありますか。
examples.en: Do you have a cheaper one?

examples.jp: 部屋[へや]は静[しず]かな{の}がいいです。
examples.en: For the room, I'd like a quiet one.

examples.jp: 昨日[きのう]買[か]った{の}はどこですか。
examples.en: Where's the one I bought yesterday?

examples.jp: 大[おお]きい{の}と小[ちい]さい{の}、どちらにしますか。
examples.en: Which will you have, the big one or the small one?

contrast.note: あかいものを ください asks for something red in general; あかいのを ください picks the red one out of the ones in view.
こと is a matter or a fact, never a physical object. For "the one" you can pick up, use の.
For a person, say せの たかい ひと, not せの たかいの: の for people sounds dismissive.

mistakes.bad: これは私[わたし]{の}のです。
mistakes.good: これは私[わたし]{の}です。
mistakes.note: "Mine" is a single の; the possessive の already stands in for the noun.

mistakes.bad: 静[しず]か{の}がいいです。
mistakes.good: 静[しず]かな{の}がいいです。
mistakes.note: な-adjectives keep な before the pronoun の, exactly as before a noun.

skills.tip: English "one" standing in for a noun, or "mine" / "yours"? The Japanese says の.

skills.rule: Inside a clause that describes a noun, the subject can take の instead of が.
skills.explain:
In a relative clause (a verb or adjective clause placed before a noun), the subject is normally marked が, but の is just as correct: 母が作った料理 and 母の作った料理 both mean "the food my mother made". This is common with short descriptive clauses: 背の高い人 "a tall person", 目の大きい猫, 雨の降る日.

It only works before a noun. At the end of a sentence the subject must be が: 母が作りました, never 母の作りました. Nouns like 時 and 日 count, so 雨の降る時 is fine.

Keep が when the clause also has a を object. 田中さんが手紙を書いた日 is clear, but with の the listener reads 田中さんの手紙 "Mr Tanaka's letter" first. The subject inside a relative clause never takes は.

How to tell it from the possessive: after this の comes a verb or adjective, not the noun it describes.

examples.jp: 背[せ]{の}高[たか]い人[ひと]は誰[だれ]ですか。
examples.en: Who is the tall person?

examples.jp: 目[め]{の}大[おお]きい猫[ねこ]を飼[か]っています。
examples.en: I have a cat with big eyes.

examples.jp: 母[はは]{の}作[つく]った料理[りょうり]が一番[いちばん]好[す]きです。
examples.en: I like the food my mother makes best of all.

examples.jp: 雨[あめ]{の}降[ふ]る日[ひ]は家[いえ]にいます。
examples.en: On rainy days I stay at home.

examples.jp: 友達[ともだち]{の}住[す]んでいる町[まち]は静[しず]かです。
examples.en: The town where my friend lives is quiet.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さん{の}書[か]いた本[ほん]を読[よ]みましたか。
examples.en: Have you read the book Mr Tanaka wrote?

contrast.note: が is always possible here and is the safe default; の is the lighter, very common variant in short clauses. Outside a noun-describing clause, only が works.
は never marks the subject inside a relative clause: せは たかい ひと is wrong. は belongs to the main sentence.
たなかさんの ほん is Mr Tanaka's book; たなかさんの かいた ほん is the book Mr Tanaka wrote. A verb right after の means it is the subject.

mistakes.bad: この料理[りょうり]は母[はは]{の}作[つく]りました。
mistakes.good: この料理[りょうり]は母[はは]{が}作[つく]りました。
mistakes.note: の can replace が only in a clause in front of a noun, not in the main sentence.

mistakes.bad: 背[せ]{は}高[たか]い人[ひと]が好[す]きです。
mistakes.good: 背[せ]{の}高[たか]い人[ひと]が好[す]きです。
mistakes.note: The subject of a describing clause takes の or が, never は.

mistakes.bad: 田中[たなか]さん{の}手紙[てがみ]を書[か]いた日[ひ]を覚[おぼ]えています。
mistakes.good: 田中[たなか]さん{が}手紙[てがみ]を書[か]いた日[ひ]を覚[おぼ]えています。
mistakes.note: With a を object in the clause, の reads as "Mr Tanaka's letter"; keep が.

skills.tip: の followed by a verb or adjective, then a noun? It is が in disguise: swap in が, and if the sentence still means the same, it is the subject.

skills.rule: End with んです when the sentence explains something or asks for an explanation.
skills.explain:
んです (written のです, casual んだ or の) wraps the sentence up as background: "the thing is...". Use it to give a reason or excuse (頭が痛いんです "I have a headache, that's why"), to ask about something you have noticed (どうしたんですか "What's wrong?"), and to lead into a request (道を聞きたいんですが...). The verb or い-adjective before it is in plain form, past included (止まっていたんです); a noun or な-adjective takes な (学生なんです, 静かなんです).

A question with んですか assumes there is something to explain: 行くんですか means "So you're going?", 行きますか is a neutral "Are you going?". Overuse sounds insistent; for a plain fact nobody asked about, use です or ます.

In casual speech, the question is just の with rising intonation (どうしたの？), and statements use んだ.

examples.jp: 頭[あたま]が痛[いた]い{んです}。
examples.en: I have a headache, that's why.

examples.jp: どうした{んです}か。
examples.en: What's wrong?

examples.jp: 明日[あした]、試験[しけん]がある{んです}。
examples.en: I have an exam tomorrow, you see.

examples.jp: 日曜日[にちようび]は休[やす]みな{んです}か。
examples.en: So you're off on Sundays?

examples.jp: 遅[おく]れてすみません。電車[でんしゃ]が止[と]まっていた{んです}。
examples.en: Sorry I'm late. The trains had stopped.

examples.jp: すみません、駅[えき]に行[い]きたい{んです}が、道[みち]を教[おし]えてもらえますか。
examples.en: Excuse me, I'm trying to get to the station. Could you tell me the way?

contrast.note: いたいです reports a fact; いたいんです offers it as the reason behind something (being late, leaving early, looking unwell).
いきますか asks for information; いくんですか asks you to confirm or explain something you have noticed, such as a packed bag.
よ pushes new information at the listener; んです explains the situation. They combine: いくんですよ "I'm going, you see".

mistakes.bad: 弟[おとうと]はまだ学生[がくせい]{んです}。
mistakes.good: 弟[おとうと]はまだ学生[がくせい]な{んです}。
mistakes.note: After a noun or な-adjective, んです needs な.

mistakes.bad: 頭[あたま]が痛[いた]いな{んです}。
mistakes.good: 頭[あたま]が痛[いた]い{んです}。
mistakes.note: い-adjectives and verbs attach directly; な is only for nouns and な-adjectives.

skills.tip: Could you add "that's why" or "so...?" in English? Then end with んです.
